agent_reason: Both are risk-bearing specialty commercial P&C insurers. They sell to businesses in niche industries such as transportation and nonprofit, and the sites describe decentralized specialty units. Both earn premiums plus investment income. Old Republic also has a title insurance line, but its specialty commercial insurance covers the target's whole business.

Both are risk-bearing specialty commercial property and casualty insurers. AFG's Specialty P&C Group includes a Specialty Casualty grouping, and Bowhead writes casualty, professional liability and healthcare liability. Both sell to commercial businesses and nonprofits, and both earn premiums plus investment income. The product overlap is real but not complete: AFG is broader (property and transportation, specialty financial), while Bowhead is narrower and focused on casualty and professional lines.

Both are P&C insurance carriers earning premiums plus investment income and selling through independent agents and brokers. AFG writes specialty commercial lines nationally for businesses. Kingstone mainly writes personal lines, mostly homeowners, in the Northeast. The only product overlap is a small commercial auto line at Kingstone. The customers are mostly different, so this is adjacent.

Both are risk-bearing specialty commercial property and casualty insurers. They underwrite niche commercial coverages (casualty, property, financial lines) for business customers placed through agents and brokers. They earn money from premiums and investment income. The target is larger and more diversified, with crop and transportation lines. The comp is a narrower small-business E&S carrier. The product and customer overlap is still direct.

Both are risk-bearing property and casualty carriers. They sell commercial specialty insurance through agents and brokers and earn premiums plus investment income. AFG is a diversified national specialty writer across more than 35 businesses. It writes casualty, transportation, crop and financial lines as well as property. The comp is a Florida-only writer of catastrophe-exposed commercial residential property (condo, HOA, apartment and assisted living). Only the commercial property line overlaps, and the buyers are a narrow, Florida-based real estate segment, so this is adjacent, not direct.

AFG is a risk-bearing specialty commercial P&C insurer. It earns underwriting premiums and investment income, and it sells through independent agents and brokers. Goosehead is a personal-lines insurance agency and franchisor. It earns carrier commissions and franchise royalties and fees, and it sells home and auto policies to individual consumers. The two share only the broad P&C insurance label. Goosehead is closer to a distribution channel that AFG might use than to a competitor.

AFG is a risk-bearing specialty P&C insurer. It underwrites policies and earns premiums plus investment income. Brown & Brown is an insurance intermediary. It places coverage for clients and earns commissions and fees without carrying underwriting risk. Both serve commercial insurance buyers, but they make money in different ways. Brown & Brown also sells to individuals and handles employee benefits. In the value chain, Brown & Brown is a distribution channel for carriers like AFG.

AFG underwrites specialty commercial property and casualty insurance (specialty casualty, property and transportation, specialty financial) for businesses. Stewart sells title insurance and escrow and closing services tied to real estate transactions. The two products are different. Customers are different too: AFG sells to commercial policyholders, and Stewart sells to homebuyers, lenders and real estate professionals. Both are regulated insurers that earn premiums and sell through agents, but that shared model is not enough to make them peers.

AFG is a specialty P&C insurance carrier that underwrites commercial risk and earns premiums plus investment income. Baldwin is an insurance distributor and advisor that earns commissions and fees. It places coverage with carriers for businesses and individuals, and it also sells personal insurance, benefits and wealth management. The two sit in the same industry but along different parts of the value chain. Baldwin is closer to a distribution channel for carriers like AFG than to a competitor.

Both are insurance underwriters earning premiums and investment income, with high state insurance regulation. But AFG sells commercial specialty P&C to businesses via brokers. Security National sells life/pre-need insurance, title insurance and mortgages, mostly to consumers and real estate and funeral channels, and owns funeral homes. The overlap is only the general insurance model.

Both companies work on protecting metal and infrastructure assets with coatings, and both sell to industrial and infrastructure customers. AZZ is a service provider that applies zinc and coil coatings to customer steel. PPG is a global manufacturer of paints and coatings across many markets, including architectural, automotive and aerospace. The overlap is partial on both product and customers, and the business model differs. PPG is closer to a coatings supplier than a competitor, so I grade it adjacent.

AZZ sells galvanizing and coil coating as a service on customer-owned steel, plus coated coil. Perma-Pipe manufactures engineered pre-insulated piping, containment and leak detection systems for specific projects. Its anti-corrosion coating is applied to its own pipe and is not sold as a stand-alone coating service. End markets overlap only loosely (infrastructure and industrial). Buyers differ: AZZ sells to fabricators and coil users, Perma-Pipe to district energy, mechanical and pipeline contractors.

AZZ sells hot-dip galvanizing and coil coating, which are metal coating services and coated coil. IES is an electrical and mechanical contractor with custom power equipment, and it is adding structural steel through DBM Global. IES has no coating offering. Both serve infrastructure and industrial markets, but their products and revenue models differ. AZZ earns service fees on customer-owned steel and sells coated coil. IES earns money from installation contracts.

Textron overlaps with Butler National's aerospace side: special mission aircraft, avionics and aircraft service, sold to business-aviation operators and militaries. Butler National also runs a material casino and gaming management business, and Textron has nothing like it. Textron is also a diversified OEM that builds whole aircraft, helicopters and industrial vehicles. Butler National is a modification, avionics and electronics supplier. A comp that matches only one of the target's material businesses gets at most 1.

Both do FAA-certified aircraft modifications and avionics work for aircraft operators. AerSale's main business is used aircraft, engine and parts sales, leasing and MRO. Butler National also makes defense electronics and owns and manages casinos, and AerSale has nothing like that. The comp therefore matches only one of the target's material businesses, which caps the score at 1.

Butler National is mainly an aerospace business (aircraft modifications, avionics, defense electronics) that also owns Boot Hill Casino and manages gaming and hospitality. Red Rock Resorts owns and operates casinos in the Las Vegas valley and used to manage a tribal casino. The two overlap only in casino and hospitality operations and casino management, which is one of the target's material businesses. Red Rock has no aerospace business and sells only to consumers. A comp that matches one of several businesses gets at most 1.

Butler National is mainly an aerospace holding company (aircraft modifications, avionics, defense electronics). It also runs a gaming and hospitality segment built around Boot Hill Casino. Monarch is a pure casino resort operator in Reno and Black Hawk. That makes Monarch a match for only the casino segment. It has no overlap with the aerospace business, and its customers are leisure and gaming guests rather than OEMs and governments. Because it matches only one of the target's material businesses, the score is capped at 1.

Butler National is mainly an aerospace holding company (FAA-approved aircraft modifications, avionics, defense electronics) with a smaller gaming and hospitality segment that manages Boot Hill Casino. Century Casinos owns and operates casinos, hotels and restaurants for leisure guests. Century overlaps only with Butler's casino segment, so the match covers one of the target's material businesses. It doesn't touch the aerospace business, which sells to OEMs, militaries and operators. That caps the score at 1.

Butler National is a diversified holding company. Its aerospace units (Avcon aircraft modifications and avionics integration, BNC Tempe defense electronics) overlap with Innovative Aerosystems. Both design FAA-certified avionics and sell to OEMs, operators and the military. Butler also runs a material gaming and hospitality business (Boot Hill Casino and casino management), and the comp has no such business. A comp that matches only one of the target's material businesses gets at most 1.

Gogo overlaps only with Butler's aerospace segment. Both sell aircraft electronics and avionics-type equipment to business and government aircraft operators and OEMs. Gogo's main business is subscription inflight connectivity, which Butler does not offer. Butler also runs a casino and gaming management segment, which Gogo has nothing to match. Because only one of Butler's material businesses overlaps, the score is capped at 1.

Both companies serve commercial aviation operators, so customers overlap in part. Butler National makes and certifies aircraft modifications, avionics and electronics. It sells to OEMs, defense and government buyers, and operators. It also runs a casino and gaming management business that Willis Lease has no equivalent for. Willis Lease is an asset-heavy lessor of jet engines and aircraft that also sells used parts and manages engine maintenance. The two overlap only loosely in aviation maintenance and services. The revenue models differ: Willis earns lease rent and Butler earns product sales, modification fees and casino revenue. Product overlap is weak and customer overlap is partial, so the pair is adjacent, not direct.

Both are building-envelope manufacturers selling roofing and insulation products through distributors and contractors, so there is real overlap. Carlisle is centered on commercial single-ply roofing, polyiso insulation and weatherproofing (CCM and CWT). Owens Corning's cited evidence points to a broader and more residential mix: shingles, insulation, doors and glass-fiber nonwovens and composites. Only the polyiso facer line (C:P2.7) is directly tied to commercial roofing, and it is a component sold into that market. Product and customer overlap are both partial, so this is adjacent, not a direct competitor.

Both are US building-products manufacturers selling through distributors to contractors. Carlisle focuses on roofing, waterproofing and insulation (building envelope). CSW sells HVAC/R, plumbing and electrical accessories, architectural and firestopping products, and specialty lubricants. The product overlap is only at the edges: building components, sealants, and Carlisle's HVAC brands. Customers overlap in the trades and distributors, but CSW's core buyers are HVAC, plumbing and electrical contractors and industrial users, not roofing contractors.

Both are building-products manufacturers selling through distributors and contractors into commercial construction. Carlisle's products are roofing, waterproofing and insulation, which SPX does not make. SPX's core is HVAC equipment (cooling towers, boilers, electric heat) plus detection and measurement systems sold to utilities and transit agencies. The only product overlap is Carlisle's small HVAC brands line. Customer overlap is partial: contractors, building owners and distributors. Carlisle sells roofing contractors and SPX sells HVAC engineers and contractors, and SPX also sells to utilities and governments. This is overlap in some customers and a little in product, not both fully, so the grade is 1.

Both are manufacturers of building and protective materials sold through contractors and distributors. Carlisle makes roofing membranes, polyiso insulation and waterproofing. PPG makes paints, coatings and sealants for many end markets. The overlap is limited to the building-envelope side (coatings, sealants, construction) and a small aerospace link. PPG's evidence shows no roofing systems or insulation. Its main customers are automotive, industrial, packaging and consumers, which Carlisle does not target.

Both are building-products manufacturers selling through distributors to contractors in construction. Carlisle sells building envelope products: roofing membranes, polyiso insulation and waterproofing. Simpson sells structural connectors, anchors and fasteners. The customers overlap, but the products are different and serve different functions (envelope vs. structural). That makes them adjacent, not direct competitors.

Both are US-centric manufacturers of building products sold through distributors to contractors and building owners for commercial new-build and retrofit work, so the business model and end market overlap. The products differ. Carlisle makes roofing membranes, insulation and weatherproofing for the building envelope. Zurn Elkay makes plumbing, drinking water, drainage and flow-control products. The buyers are different trades: roofing contractors and roofing distributors versus plumbing wholesalers and engineers. That leaves the customer overlap partial and the product overlap weak, so this is adjacent rather than direct.

Carlisle manufactures building envelope products (roofing membranes, insulation, waterproofing) sold through distributors and contractors. Comfort Systems USA is a mechanical/electrical/plumbing contractor that installs and services building systems on a project and service basis. Both serve commercial construction, but one makes and sells products and the other sells installation labor and services.

The target runs a fleet of concrete pumps with operators and earns fees per job or hour. It also provides concrete washout waste services to construction contractors. DXP is an MRO industrial distributor. It sells supplies, bearings and pumps, plus repair and supply-chain services, mainly to industrial, energy and manufacturing customers. The word "pump" is the only link, and the products are unrelated: DXP's pumps are industrial rotating equipment, while the target places concrete. The business models differ too: DXP distributes and repairs, and the target operates a service fleet.

Target is a service and rental operator that places concrete with its own pump fleet and operators, and also runs concrete waste removal. Comp manufactures and sells water, wastewater, fire and industrial pumps through distributors. The only link is the word pump, plus a small construction customer overlap.

Target provides concrete pumping and concrete washout waste services to construction contractors. The comp provides fire protection, security, elevator, HVAC and specialty infrastructure inspection, maintenance and installation services to building owners. The offerings do not overlap. Customers overlap only loosely, at the level of commercial and industrial construction and facilities. Both are branch-based service businesses, but that is too generic to count.
